reason: The hypothesis relies on general textbook knowledge about alumina's protective properties, but the two cited passages (E1 and E2) do not provide any specific prior evidence for the key premises. E1 discusses hot corrosion of high-entropy alloy coatings in molten sulfate/chloride salts, and E2 discusses corrosion of a high-entropy alloy in molten fluoride salt; neither addresses pre-oxidation of borides, formation of alumina scales, or corrosion resistance in molten aluminum. The premises are therefore unsupported by the cited evidence.
premises: Alumina (Al2O3) is chemically stable and has low diffusivity at elevated temperatures, making it an effective diffusion barrier.
A thin, continuous alumina scale can be formed on a substrate by pre-oxidation in air at ~800 °C.
The alumina scale will prevent direct contact and interdiffusion between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
This barrier effect will significantly reduce dissolution of boride constituents and lower the corrosion rate compared to untreated boride components.
